lead: A VANET (vehicular ad hoc network) is a wireless network that moving vehicles form among themselves. Links appear as cars come into radio range and vanish as they part; roadside units (RSUs) can add fixed access points, but vehicles can still pass messages car to car where there is none. Because cars move fast but only along roads, and every car knows its own position from satellite navigation, a VANET routes packets by position instead of by stored routes. Only a few universities teach this in depth.
prereq: You need the V2X links, OBUs and RSUs from V2X communication.

sections.h3: Ad hoc networks and the three VANET domains

blocks.text: An ad hoc network has no fixed infrastructure: every node forwards packets for the others, so distant nodes reach each other in several hops. A VANET is a special ad hoc network whose nodes are vehicles, each with an on-board unit (OBU). Its architecture has three domains. The in-vehicle domain is the car's own ECUs and buses, joined to the OBU through the gateway. The ad hoc domain is OBU-to-OBU and OBU-to-RSU radio. The infrastructure domain is the RSUs' wired back-haul, the internet and the servers behind it.

Road crashes kill about 1.19 million people a year worldwide, according to the WHO's 2023 global status report, most of them in low- and middle-income countries such as India. Safety applications aim at this: collision warning, hazard and crash warning, intersection warning and emergency-vehicle warning. Non-safety applications include traffic information, electronic tolling, parking, fleet tracking and infotainment. Safety messages are short, repeated and urgent; non-safety messages can wait.

VANETs differ from general mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs): nodes move fast, so links last seconds; motion follows roads, so it is predictable; vehicles have plenty of battery power and space; position and time come from GNSS; and the network can be huge in a jam yet broken into pieces on an empty highway at night. Their challenges are frequent link breaks, the broadcast storm (many cars rebroadcasting the same alert and jamming the channel), GNSS errors in tunnels and between tall buildings, security against fake messages, and drivers' privacy.

Topology-based routing finds and stores a path. AODV (ad hoc on-demand distance vector) floods a route request and keeps the route found; DSR (dynamic source routing) puts the whole path in each packet. At road speeds the links break before a route can be repaired, so these work poorly. Position-based routing needs only the positions of the neighbours and of the destination. GPSR (greedy perimeter stateless routing) first uses greedy forwarding: send the packet to the neighbour closest to the destination. If no neighbour is closer than the current node (a void), it switches to perimeter mode: face routing with the right-hand rule on a planarized graph of the radio neighbours (a Gabriel or relative neighbourhood graph), until it reaches a node closer than where greedy forwarding stopped. Delivery is guaranteed only if that graph is connected.

Geocast sends a message to every vehicle inside a target area, such as 1 km behind a crash; it suppresses the broadcast storm by letting only the farthest receiver rebroadcast, or by random waiting. Where no next car exists, store-carry-forward keeps the packet in a car until another car or an RSU comes into range.

examples.question: A packet at a car at (0, 0) m must reach a destination at (100, 0) m. The car's neighbours are A at (40, 10), B at (70, −20) and C at (20, 30). Which neighbour does greedy forwarding choose?
steps: For each neighbour (x, y), distance to the destination d = √((100 − x)² + (0 − y)²).
The current car is 100 m from the destination; B is the closest neighbour and is closer than 100 m, so greedy mode continues.
examples.answer: Greedy forwarding sends the packet to B, 36.1 m from the destination.

examples.question: Radio range is 250 m. (a) Two cars on opposite carriageways each drive at 120 km/h. For how long can they exchange messages as they pass? (b) Two cars in the same lane drive at 100 km/h and 80 km/h, starting side by side. How long until the link breaks?
steps: They are in range from 250 m before meeting to 250 m after: 500 m of relative travel. Time = 500 ÷ 66.7 = 7.5 s.
The link breaks when the gap reaches 250 m: 250 ÷ 5.56 = 45 s.
examples.answer: (a) about 7.5 s; (b) about 45 s. Links with oncoming traffic are short, so a route through them must be rebuilt every few seconds.

traps: VANET nodes are not energy-limited and do not move randomly; MANET assumptions of battery limits and random motion do not hold.
Greedy forwarding picks the neighbour closest to the destination, not the one closest to the sender or the farthest away.
Perimeter mode uses a planarized graph of radio neighbours, not the road map; delivery is guaranteed only if that graph is connected.
Flooding a hazard alert is not free: unchecked rebroadcasting causes the broadcast storm.

quiz.q: Name the three domains of a VANET architecture.
quiz.a: In-vehicle domain, ad hoc domain and infrastructure domain.

quiz.q: Give two safety and two non-safety VANET applications.
quiz.a: Safety: collision warning, intersection warning. Non-safety: electronic tolling, traffic information.

quiz.q: Why does road-constrained motion help routing?
quiz.a: Cars follow roads and know their position, so future positions are predictable and a packet can be sent towards a place rather than along a stored route.

quiz.q: A neighbour is at (60, 80) m and the destination at (100, 0) m. Find its distance to the destination.
Range 300 m; oncoming cars each at 90 km/h. Find the contact time.
quiz.a: Closing speed 180 km/h = 50 m/s; 600 m ÷ 50 = 12 s.

quiz.q: Why does AODV perform badly at 120 km/h?
quiz.a: Links last only seconds, so routes break before repair finishes; each new route request floods the network, adding delay and load, and packets are lost meanwhile.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research uses traffic simulators such as SUMO with network simulators to test routing, and newer work uses cellular and edge servers for most non-safety traffic. Search for SUMO and Veins, geocast routing and VANET security.
